CausalChain: Heavy alcohol intake -> Disruption of gut microbiota (↓ butyrate producers, ↑ LPS) -> Increased intestinal permeability -> Translocation of LPS to liver -> Activation of Kupffer cells and pro-inflammatory cytokine production (e.g., TNF, IL-6) -> Hepatic inflammation and fibrogenesis -> Progression to cirrhosis and HCC; Dietary prebiotics -> Augmentation of butyrate-producing bacteria -> Restoration of gut barrier integrity -> Reduced LPS translocation -> Attenuation of hepatic inflammatory signals -> Lower risk of cirrhosis progressing to HCC
Hypothesis: Supplementation with dietary prebiotics that enrich butyrate-producing gut bacteria will ameliorate alcohol-induced liver inflammation by restoring intestinal barrier function, thereby reducing the progression from alcohol-associated cirrhosis to hepatocellular carcinoma.
Abstract: Alcohol consumption is a well‐recognized driver of liver inflammation and hepatocarcinogenesis, acting through both direct hepatic metabolism and indirect pathways such as gut microbial dysbiosis. We propose a novel hypothesis that targeted modulation of the gut microbiota through dietary prebiotics to boost butyrate‐producing bacteria can restore intestinal barrier integrity, reduce translocation of bacterial endotoxins like lipopolysaccharide (LPS), and subsequently diminish the inflammatory cascade within the liver. This may ultimately mitigate the progression from alcohol‐associated cirrhosis to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
